solution:
The wrong pair is (4) Jyoti Mhapsekar – Women's Commission.

The chapter connects Jyoti Mhapsekar not with any Women's Commission but with the street play Mulgi Jhaali Ho, which was one of the programmes that grew out of the work of the Stree-mukti Sangharsha Samiti.

The other three pairs are correct. Soudamini Rao established the Streemukti Andolan Samiti in Pune in 1977; Vidya Bal's work included the Nari Samata Manch along with her periodicals and Milun Saryajani; and Pramila Dandavate established the Mahila Dakshata Samiti in Delhi in 1976.

Women had taken part in the freedom struggle in large numbers and went on contributing in every field after independence, yet the roots of many of the problems they faced still lay in a male-centred mentality that society had not rid itself of. Everyday hardships brought this discontent into the open: shortages of oil, ghee, rava and maida just before Diwali and the high price of kerosene led the women of Mumbai to come out in 1972 in the laatne morcha under the leadership of the socialist leader Mrinal Gore, and its success gave the public a glimpse of the united power of women. Support also came from outside the country, as the United Nations declared 1975 as the International Women's Year with the three aims of peace, development and equality between men and women. In the same year the government of India set up the Committee on the Status of Women under Dr Phulrenu Guha, whose comprehensive survey of women's social position, education, wages, working conditions and the female-male ratio showed clearly how far behind women had been left. Against this background a State-wide conference of women was organised in 1975 by the Stree-mukti Sangharsha Samiti, which published its manifesto in 1978 and adopted the policy of struggling against discrimination based on gender, caste and varna. In this way the women's liberation movement began.

The Dowry Prohibition Act of 1961 had already made both the giving and the taking of dowry a cognizable criminal offence, but the practice did not stop. Even after this law, incidents kept being reported in which a woman was said to have burnt to death when her sari pallu caught fire while cooking, or to have slipped into a well while washing clothes and drowned. Investigations showed that dowry was in fact the most frequent cause of such deaths, and the role played in these cases by the police, the administration and the judiciary was highlighted. This created much greater public awareness of how women were being harmed, and as a result the Dowry Prohibition (Amendment) Act came into force in 1984. The seriousness of the problem can be judged from the figures the chapter gives: 2209 women died as victims of the dowry tradition in 1988, 4835 in 1990 and 5377 in 1993.

In the post-independence period our Constitution adopted the values of freedom, equality, fraternity and social justice. The practice of untouchability went completely against these values, because it denied a whole section of society the equality and dignity the Constitution had promised to every citizen. In accordance with these values, therefore, untouchability was banned by law and was removed by the 17th paragraph of the Constitution. The class that had suffered under this practice was included in the Scheduled Castes. Since these castes had been kept educationally and socially backward, they were also given reservations in education and in jobs so that their development could be made easier.

A minority means a group of people of a particular religion, language or race who are few in number in a society. Our country has many religions, sects and languages, so there is great cultural diversity and a great variation in cultural traditions. If such small groups are to preserve their cultural traditions and develop their own language, they need protection, and so the Constitution gives citizens certain educational and cultural rights. Minorities have the right to protect and conserve their language, culture and traditions, and for this purpose they also have the right to set up separate educational institutions. The government implements various schemes for their progress.

The Chipko movement of 1973 was another show of constructive woman power. Trees in the forests in the foothills of the Himalayas were to be cut down for commercial purposes, and Chandiprasad Bhat and Sunderlal Bahuguna started a movement to prevent this. Women joined in large numbers and followed the strategy of holding hands and encircling each tree; because their method was to protect a tree by embracing it, the movement came to be known as the Chipko movement. Women had a big role to play in the agricultural economy of that region, and it was the activist Gaura Devi who created this awareness among them with the help of Sudesha Devi and Bachani Devi.

The Protection of Human Rights Act was enacted in 1993 to prevent injustice to men and women. The National Human Rights Commission was formed for this purpose, and in some States a State Human Rights Commission was formed on the same lines. The law deals with matters such as collective oppression, the social conditions of divorced women, and women and secure work places. It played an effective role in mitigating injustices to women.

When women act together, their united strength has brought about constructive changes in many fields.

In the economic field, the women of Mumbai showed this strength in 1972. Facing the brunt of scarcity of supplies and rising prices, with commodities like oil, ghee, rava and maida becoming scarce just before Diwali and kerosene becoming very expensive, they came together brandishing their rolling pins under the leadership of the socialist leader Mrinal Gore in the demonstration known as the laatne morcha. The movement met with success and the public got a glimpse of the united power of women.

In the field of protection of the environment, women showed the same strength in the Chipko movement of 1973. When trees in the forests in the foothills of the Himalayas were to be cut down for commercial purposes, women held hands and encircled each tree to protect it, and Gaura Devi created this awareness among them with the help of Sudesha Devi and Bachani Devi.

In social reform, the anti-liquor movement that began in Andhra Pradesh in 1992 is a clear example. After three youths of Dubuganta village in Nellore district drowned in a lake in a state of inebriation, the women of the village came together and forced the closure of the arrack shops. The report of this in the local newspapers had its effect on many other villages, the movement spread to the entire State, and the government had to adopt a strict policy against the sale of alcohol.

Women also worked through organisations. The Stree-mukti Sangharsha Samiti organised a State-wide conference in 1975 and published its manifesto in 1978, adopting the policy of struggle against discrimination based on gender, caste and varna. Pramila Dandavate established the Mahila Dakshata Samiti in Delhi in 1976 and its branches came up in several States, while the Akhil Bharatiya Janavadi Mahila Sanghatana, established in 1980, began a struggle against dowry, female foeticide and domestic abuse. Anti-dowry protection committees were formed all over Maharashtra.

Women also brought about change in the fields of law and education. The women activists and journalists Meena Menon, Geeta Seshu, Sujata Anandan, Anu Joseph and Kalpana Sharma investigated the case in which Roop Kanwar was coerced into committing sati, and in 1988 the government passed the Sati (Prevention) Act with very stringent provisions. Women's Studies Centres started at the SNDT Women's University, the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Savitribai Phule Pune University and Shivaji University played an important role in the critical analysis of women's issues. All these examples show that when women unite, they can win constructive change in the economy, the environment, social customs, law and education alike.
